title: Quality and Research Analysts: series plan

criteria.check: The series has a clear name and premise that tell a viewer why to watch all of it.
criteria.why: A series sells as a whole.

criteria.check: Episode 1 is the strongest, most clickable story, not just the chronologically first.
criteria.why: The first episode decides whether a series is found.

criteria.check: The order has a pull: big and smaller stories alternate, one of the strongest is saved for the end, and a shared timeline is kept unless the opening breaks it.
Every episode stands alone: one strong question of its own, answerable in one video.
criteria.why: Most viewers arrive at a random episode.

criteria.check: Formats and settings vary across the series where the material allows.
criteria.why: Three a week of the same shape feels repetitive.

criteria.check: Every topic has enough concrete, sourceable material for the requested length and no more (70-90 beats for 10 minutes).
criteria.why: Thin topics pad; huge ones rush.

criteria.check: Each synopsis gives the angle, the question, the beats in order, names, dates, places, the turn and the payoff: enough for the producer to work from alone.
criteria.why: The synopsis is the episode producer's whole brief.

criteria.check: Every episode has a clear era and things that can be shown; none hinges on identifiable private people, graphic violence or unsourceable claims.
criteria.why: The pictures and the facts must both be possible.

criteria.check: No two episodes cover the same event or answer the same question.
criteria.why: Overlap wastes an episode and bores returning viewers.

criteria.check: series/research.md lists the candidates considered, why each was kept or dropped, and sources for each kept topic.
criteria.why: The reviewer needs to see the choice was informed.

criteria.check: When the series style or palette was chosen automatically, it suits most of the episodes' tone and eras, not only the first.
criteria.why: Every episode is made with it.
